marketFearBreadth.pageTitle: What is market fear breadth? How many stocks are at extreme lows
marketFearBreadth.pageDescription: Market fear breadth tells you how many holdings are sitting at extreme fear at the same time. A single stock falling to extreme fear and the whole market falling to extreme fear are different things. Updated after each close for Taiwan and the US.
marketFearBreadth.keywords: market fear breadth,market breadth,how many stocks at lows,LOHAS five-line,extreme fear,Taiwan market sentiment,US market sentiment
marketFearBreadth.heading: What is market fear breadth? How many stocks are at extreme lows
marketFearBreadth.lede: One stock falling to extreme fear and the whole market falling to extreme fear are different things. Market fear breadth measures how many holdings in a fixed list are sitting at extreme fear right now.
marketFearBreadth.whatItIs: We run the LOHAS five-line analysis over a fixed list of holdings and count how many have fallen more than two standard deviations below their trend line — the position labelled "extreme fear" across the site. Dividing that count by the number we can evaluate that day gives the breadth. The US list is 28 ETFs covering major countries and sectors; Taiwan uses 38 large caps spanning industries.
marketFearBreadth.howToRead: When the number climbs noticeably, it means it is no longer one holding panicking — the whole market is.

bands.meaning: Only isolated holdings are at an extreme. Market sentiment overall is normal.

bands.range: Elevated (above 25% in the US, above 16% in Taiwan)
bands.meaning: Higher than on roughly nine out of ten historical days, indicating fear has spread across more assets. This is a historical rank, not a 90% share of assets.
Usually the whole market falling together. Historically, when this has triggered, the year that followed was the strongest — though price typically fell further first.

marketFearBreadth.history: US history starts in 1996 and Taiwan history in 2000. The 90th historical percentile means breadth is higher than on roughly nine out of ten observed days—not that 90% of assets are at Extreme Fear. Extreme readings can persist.
marketFearBreadth.relationToSioTitle: Using it alongside a single stock
marketFearBreadth.relationToSio: On a stock’s LOHAS five-line page, when that stock is already at extreme fear, the status row also shows how broad the market’s fear is that day. You can see whether only this one holding has reached extreme fear, or the whole market with it.
marketFearBreadth.source: Calculated by Sentiment Inside Out from public market data. Updated every trading day for Taiwan and the US.

taiwanFearGreed.pageTitle: What is the Taiwan Fear & Greed Index and how do you read it?
taiwanFearGreed.pageDescription: A full guide to the Taiwan Fear & Greed Index: a 0-to-100 sentiment gauge for Taiwan equities built from local data including TAIFEX options volatility, put/call ratio, margin ratios and market breadth, updated every trading day.
taiwanFearGreed.keywords: taiwan fear and greed index,taiwan stock sentiment,TAIEX sentiment,taiwan VIX,TAIFEX,margin ratio,taiwan market sentiment
taiwanFearGreed.heading: What is the Taiwan Fear & Greed Index and how do you read it?
taiwanFearGreed.lede: The Taiwan Fear & Greed Index describes on a 0-to-100 scale whether Taiwan equity investors currently lean fearful or greedy. It is calculated entirely from local market data covering options volatility, margin financing, foreign investor positioning and market breadth, updated every trading day.
taiwanFearGreed.whatItIsTitle: What is the Taiwan Fear & Greed Index?
taiwanFearGreed.whatItIs: Nearly every well-known sentiment gauge is built for US equities, which leaves Taiwan investors applying tools designed for a different market structure. Retail participation, the margin financing system and the weight of foreign institutional flows all differ from the US, so borrowing US readings directly invites misreads. This index uses Taiwan data instead: TAIFEX options volatility, the options put/call ratio, margin maintenance and short-to-margin ratios, market breadth, foreign futures positioning, the exchange rate and TAIEX momentum, each standardised against its own long history before being combined.
taiwanFearGreed.howToReadTitle: How do you read the Taiwan Fear & Greed Index?
taiwanFearGreed.howToRead: Lower means more panic, higher means more optimism. Because each input is standardised over a long window, an extreme reading means extreme relative to more than two decades of history rather than just the past few months.

bands.meaning: Extreme Fear. The market leans defensive.
Neutral. Sentiment is not strongly tilted either way.
Extreme Greed. Sentiment is running hot.

taiwanFearGreed.historyTitle: Historical range of the Taiwan Fear & Greed Index
taiwanFearGreed.history: The series goes back to July 2001 with more than six thousand daily readings, covering two decades of Taiwan bull and bear cycles and reaching both ends of the 0-to-100 range. Note that TAIFEX options volatility data begins only in November 2016, so readings before that rest on the remaining components, which is worth bearing in mind when interpreting early values.
taiwanFearGreed.relationToSioTitle: How Taiwan sentiment differs from US sentiment
taiwanFearGreed.relationToSio: Taiwan and US sentiment frequently move out of step. Taiwan is heavily shaped by foreign institutional flows, the exchange rate and the electronics cycle, none of which appear in US gauges. Watching both reveals whether money is de-risking globally or repositioning within a single market.
taiwanFearGreed.relationToSioCta: View the Taiwan Fear & Greed Index
taiwanFearGreed.source: Taiwan Stock Exchange and Taiwan Futures Exchange public data, calculated by Sentiment Inside Out. Updated every trading day.
